6.128.m: Vasiṣṭha said: / Listen about the piśācas who were released by him in that forest. / Formerly there was a king named Citra in the Drāviḍa country,
in the lunar dynasty, a great warrior, heroic, master of weapons and missiles, / equipped with hosts of elephants, horses, and chariots, always valorous.
With a treasury full of gold and jewels of various kinds, possessing vast wealth, / he always played in the midst of a thousand women, intent on them alone.
Devoted to women, lustful, ever greedy, and of fierce anger, that king / did not follow the righteous counsel offered by his ministers.
He reviled Viṣṇu excessively and ever hated the Vaiṣṇavas: / “Who is this Viṣṇu? Where was he seen? Where does he abide? By whom is he praised?”
Thus, deluded by fate, that king could not endure Viṣṇu; / he became enraged and oppressed those who worshipped Nārāyaṇa.
Established in heretical conduct, he did not acknowledge brāhmaṇas, / nor the Vedas, nor Vedic rites, nor vows, nor did he think of giving gifts.
Through injustice and fierce punishments he oppressed his subjects— / harsh, pitiless, cruel, and averse to righteous deeds.
Fallen from good conduct, hating Acyuta, neglecting the sacred fire, and fallen from ritual duties, / that king ruled the people like a second form of Death.
Then, after a great length of time, that king met his death; / he obtained no funeral rites according to Vedic ordinance.
Then, intensely tormented by the host of Yama’s servants, / [he went] on a path full of iron spikes, filled with boiling sand,
scorched by the rays of the fierce sun, devoid of the shade of trees, / strewn with glowing coals, and filled with flames of fire,
struck by extremely dreadful ravens with beaks of iron, / and devoured by terrible wolves and frightful dogs with ferocious fangs.
Hearing the weeping of other men who had committed sins, / the king went to the terrifying world of the End-Maker.
Hear, O king, his most unbearable fate in that realm: / from hell to hell that monarch went in succession.
First he went to Tāmisra, dreadful and bringing abundant pain; / and again to Andhatāmisra, where suffering is unending.
Next he went to the exceedingly fierce Mahāraurava and Raurava, / and to the hells Kālasūtra and Mahānaraka.
Afterwards, fainting from agony, that ruler was plunged into the impassable / Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tāpana, and Saṃpratāpana,
into the Pratāpa hell—his mind scorched by the fire of misery— / and into Saṃpāta, Sakākola, Kuḍūmala, and Pūtimṛttika,
into Lohaśaṅku, Mṛgīyantra, the [thorny] road, and the Śālmali river; / and then he entered the exceedingly dreadful, horrific, and impassable
Asipatravana (Sword-Leaved Forest) and Lohacāraka. / Having fallen thus into all of these, that sin-committing king
experienced torments and agonizing suffering in the terrible hell / for twenty-one cosmic ages, on account of his vocal hatred of Viṣṇu.
Having suffered the torments of Yama, the king was released from hell; / in course of time, he then became a huge piśāca upon a king of mountains.
Hungry, he roamed through all directions in that forest; / even on Mount Meru, he never found food or water.
Once, as he wandered about afflicted with grief, / the piśāca entered the Plakṣaprasravaṇa forest, destined to bear good fruit.
Taking shelter under the shade of a bibhītaka tree, exceedingly wretched, / he wept aloud, dreadfully, again and again: “Alas, I am undone!”
“Fainting from hunger and thirst, a hater of all beings— / how will an end come to this endless existence of mine?
In this ocean of sin, surrounded by waves of suffering, / who will now stretch out a supporting hand to me, who am sinking in it?”
As he was reciting, Devadyuti heard the pathetic weeping / of that piśāca whose heart was so wretched.
Approaching him there, he beheld that piśāca— / with a deformed and terrifying face, yellowish eyes, and emaciated,
with upright hair, a black body, like another messenger of Yama, / with dangling tongue, quivering lips, long shanks, and covered in veins,
with long feet, a dried-up mouth, sunken eyes, and a withered ribcage. / Then, filled with curiosity, that best of sages asked him:
Devadyuti said: / “Who are you, of terrifying form? Why do you weep so bitterly? / From where does this state arise? Speak! And what may I do for you?
Living beings who have entered my hermitage do not partake of misery; / all rejoice purely, just as in the abode of Viṣṇu.
Tell quickly, good sir, the cause of this misery of yours; / for the wise do not cause delay when a purpose is at hand.”
Vasiṣṭha said: / Hearing this speech, pleased, the piśāca ceased weeping; / bowed in humility, he then spoke in a wretched voice:
The piśāca said: / “Your words have removed the torment pervading my whole body, / just as a raining cloud removes the forest fire arising in summer on a mountain.
Whatever good deed I have, by that I have seen you, O twice-born; / for meeting with the virtuous in one place never happens to those without accumulated merit.”
Having spoken thus, he related his own past story: / "Through the fault of hatred toward Viṣṇu, I have fallen into this state."
By remembering whose name even a dying man is freed and goes to Viṣṇu’s abode— / O twice-born, vile sinner that I am, I harbored hatred against that Hari!
He who protects living beings, who is dharma in the three worlds, / and who is the inner Self of beings—against him was my hatred.
He who is sung in all the Vedas as the giver of the fruits of actions, / who is worshipped with austerities by brāhmaṇas—he became the object of my hatred.
He who is to be meditated upon in the Vedānta by ascetics who have abandoned rites, / who love the forest, are unattached and wander alone—that Hari was hated by me, O twice-born!
All the gods beginning with Brahmā, and yogis beginning with Sanaka, / worship him here for liberation; that Viṣṇu was hated by me.
He who is the eternal creator of the universe in the beginning, middle, and end, / who has neither beginning, middle, nor end—he became the object of my hatred.
Whatever good deed was performed by me in a previous birth, / all of that was consumed by the fire of hatred for Viṣṇu and reduced to ashes.
If somehow I shall see the end of this sin, / I will worship no other deity except Nārāyaṇa.
Having long suffered hellish torment because of hatred for Viṣṇu, / I came out of hell and entered the womb of a piśāca.
By what rites and mantras have I now been brought to your hermitage, / where the darkness of misery has been destroyed for me by the sun of seeing you?
Wherever death, bondage, fortune, happiness, or a wife is to be attained, / a person is dragged there by their own action as if by the neck.
Now tell me the proper action that will destroy this piśāca state; / for fortunate souls are not slow in deeds of benevolence to others.”
Devadyuti said: / “Ah, this delusion steals away the memory of gods, demons, and men, / by which even toward gods there arises hatred that destroys dharma!
He who is the creator, protector, and destroyer of the worlds, the Great Lord, / and the Self of all beings—how can any fool hate him?
By dedication to whom all actions become fruitful— / turning away from devotion to him, what mortal here does not meet a miserable fate?
Only that action prescribed by Śruti, Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous / should be practiced by the four castes, ever worshipping Nārāyaṇa.
Otherwise they go to hell, lacking adherence to the scriptures; / therefore, one should abandon actions that oppose the Vedas, even if stated in [other] texts.”
Deceiving fools here with treatises composed from their own intellect, / they obstruct the path of the highest good solely for the destruction of the world.
They revile Viṣṇu, revile the Vedas, revile asceticism and virtuous twice-born persons; / because of that, they go to hell from following bad treatises.
Just as this Drāviḍa king went to hell, / hating the god Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods and Lord of the universe.
Therefore, one who desires merit should completely abandon hatred towards the gods, especially towards the brahmins; / he should abandon any rite outside the Vedas here.
Having spoken thus, the sage explained what was beneficial to the piśāca: / "Go to Prayāga, O good sir, and observe the month of Māgha."
where your release from the state of a piśāca is certain; there is no doubt about this. / Those who bathe there go to heaven: this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
A person abandons past wicked actions there; / there is nothing anywhere else superior or greater than bathing at Prayāga.
Know Prayāga to be higher than expiation in the form of asceticism, in the form of gifts, consisting of ritual actions, / higher [even] than Vedic sacrifices and yoga, even for sinners.
That is the open gate to heaven and liberation on earth, / which is the confluence of the white and black waters; there is no other such [gate] on earth abandoning that.
It is the sole axe to cut down one who is bound in the shackles of sin. / Where is the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, Viṣṇu whose radiance is that of the sun and fire,
and where the wretched, paltry heap of sins of men, an oblation of grass? / Just as the autumn moon shines upon the destruction of dark clouds,
so a man bathed in the waters of the confluence shines after the destruction of his sins. / I am not able to tell you the glorification of the confluence of the white and black waters,
touched by a single drop of whose water a twice-born from Kerala was liberated.” / Having heard this speech of the sage, the piśāca, pleased in mind,
freed from grief as it were and delighted, affectionately asked the sage: / “How, O great sage, was that twice-born man from the Kerala country liberated?
Tell me this account, taking compassion upon me.”
Devadyuti said: / “O piśāca, hear the auspicious, holy story as I tell it: / Here in Kerala there was a brahmin named Vasu, master of the Vedas.
His wealth was seized by kinsmen, and he became destitute, abandoned by relatives; / leaving his native land, he was afflicted with great sorrow.
Wandering from country to country over a long time, / he entered a great forest, slightly afflicted by disease.
Going on toward another sacred ford, exhausted, emaciated by hunger on the Vindhya mountain, / he met death through famine, and received neither cremation nor post-death rites.
By that ripening of karma, in that very mountain cave, / having become a ghost, he dwelt for a long time in the desolate forest,
greatly tormented by cold and heat, without food, without water, / naked, without shoes, sighing with the cry: ‘Alas, alas!’
Wandering here and there, having become the wind, that twice-born of Kerala / found no refuge nor happiness anywhere at that time.
Afflicted with sorrow, he was grieving; he saw no good state at all. / He always experienced the fruit of his own action: gifts given [or not given].
Those who do not offer oblations into the fire, those who do not worship Govinda, / those who do not cultivate the knowledge of the Self, and those who turn away from excellent sacred fords,
those who do not give gold, cloth, betel, jewels, food, fruit, and water / to the distressed—they all become deprived of merit;
those who steal the property of brahmins, the property of others, and women's property, / by force or by deceit, the knaves and deceivers of others;
the hypocrites, rogues, thieves, and those who are fiery in conduct; / those who are pitiless toward children, the elderly, the sick, and women, devoid of truth;
incendiaries, poisoners, and those who give false testimony; / all those who go with women forbidden to approach, and those who sacrifice for an entire village;
and those who abandon father, mother, daughter-in-law, child, or their own wife; / those who are misers, greedy, atheists, and defilers of dharma;
those who abandon their master in battle, those who abandon one who has sought refuge; / killers of cows and confiscators of land, and others who ruin gems;
sinful slanderers of others, censurers of gods and teachers; / and those who delight in accepting gifts at all great sacred sites;
those devoted to harming others, and likewise those who harm living beings; / all those who improperly accept gifts—they are born again and again
in the degraded wombs of ghosts, rākṣasas, piśācas, animals, and trees. / There is not the slightest happiness for them in this world or the next.
Therefore, abandoning what is forbidden, one should perform prescribed actions; / one should worship sacrifice, gifts, austerity, sacred fords, mantras, God, and the teacher.
Seeing that the ripening of actions through millions of wombs is difficult to overcome, / dharma should be practiced continually by all four castes.”
Seeing that state of a ghost arisen from the seed of sin, / having imparted instruction in dharma, the twice-born spoke to him again.
“Thus, while that Kerala ghost was existing on the mountain at that time, / having spent a long time, he saw a traveler on the path,
carrying two baskets filled with water of the confluence, / singing with devotion of the god Janārdana of holy fame.
Seeing him, the ghost suddenly blocked the path; / he showed himself and said: ‘Do not fear!’
‘I desire to drink water from you, O best of pilgrims! / If you do not let me drink water, my life-breaths will surely depart.’
Hearing the words of the ghost, the traveler answered out of curiosity. / The traveler said: / "Who are you, overcome with sorrow, emaciated, pale, and naked,
with only life remaining, wishing to die, deformed, increasing fear, / having the form of fresh smoke, fierce, with trembling eyes,
your feet not touching the ground, with belly and arms devoid of flesh?" / Hearing his words, the ghost then spoke these words:
The ghost said: / ‘Hear, O most righteous one! I shall tell you how I became like this. / I was a brahmin who did not give gifts, greedy and foul in conduct;
I always ate food from others, eating sweet delicacies alone. / No alms were given by me, nor a generous portion of food;
the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice was not performed, nor was an oblation cast outside; / the thirst of beings afflicted with thirst was not quenched with water.
While roaming the earth, the ancestors were never satiated by me, / nor was a śrāddha performed anywhere, nor were the gods worshipped at all.
No protection from rain and heat, no footwear was given; / no water-pot was given by me, nor betel, nor medicine.
Shelter was not given in my house, nor hospitality shown to anyone; / the blind, elderly, penniless, helpless, and wretched were [not] satisfied with food and drink.
A mouthful was not given to cows, nor was a sick person relieved; / pure sesame seeds were not given or offered into the fire by me, O brahmin.
Givers of sesame seeds on earth do not become like me. / Nothing of great reward, like gold, was given during Vyatīpāta;
nor was anything given at the equinox or during an eclipse of the sun and moon. / All other festival days went empty for me, O twice-born.
The principal lunar days in Kārttika always became barren for me; / nothing was given to the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days and under the Maghā asterism.
Pleasure was not given to twice-born persons on the Manvantarādi and Yugādi days; / a lamp with sesame oil was not offered by me in Kārttika.
I did not bathe in the month of Māgha, which grants the desires of beauty and good fortune; / to a twice-born learned in the Vedas on the Godāvarī when Jupiter was in Leo,
the wealth that was resolved by me was not given in my previous birth; / nor did I bathe in the Kṛṣṇaveṇī when Jupiter was in Virgo.’
Kindling a fire with heaps of wood in Pauṣa and Māgha, / I did not remove the numbness of shivering brāhmaṇas who had bathed.
In the months beginning with Mādhava, I gave no cool water; / I did not plant an aśvattha tree, nor did I rear a banyan tree.
I never released living beings from prison; / I never protected one trembling with fear of creatures who came to me for refuge.
I did not please Madhusūdana here by fasting for three nights; / nor [did I perform] the kṛcchra, atikṛcchra, pārāka, or cāndrāyana [vows], O dvija,
Then other penances: the taptakṛcchra and likewise the sāṃtapanas— / these meritorious vows are practiced by gods such as Indra.
I did not emaciate my body in the past by performing them. / Thus, O best of dvijas, my previous birth proved barren.
Look, O dvija, upon this most cruel and astonishing destiny / of my past action in this birth, so hard to fathom!
There is meat on the paths, slain by wolves and tigers; / and on this mountain, there are other fruits dropped everywhere by parrots;
there are sacred, fragrant, and succulent fruits, / and roots that are very edible, soft, and sweet;
honey of various kinds abounds in great quantities; / and on every side there are waters of streams and waterfalls.
Yet although all these things are easy to find on the mountain, / I never see food anywhere, struck down as I am by fate.
I subsist on air just as serpents subsist; / yet I continue to live, O brāhmaṇa, through the power of a divine birth-state.
A person never obtains what cannot be attained / through strength, intellect, mantras, virile prowess, assistants, or friends.
In gain and loss, pleasure and pain, marriage, death, and life, / in enjoyment, illness, and separation, fate alone is indeed the cause.
The misshapen, the baseborn, fools, those censured for despicable conduct, / and those devoid of valour and heroism enjoy kingdoms through fate.
The one-eyed, the lame, the unsightly, those devoid of statecraft and full of vices, / and even eunuchs are seen established in sovereignty by fate.
Those who have given sesamum, cows, gold, and garments, / those who have given a maiden as fair as Gaurī, and those who have given the earth,
beds, seats, betel, houses, and wealth, / who have given edible foods, drinks, sandalwood, and agallochum—
in a forest, on a mountain peak, in a village, or in a city, / their pleasures wait continually before them with ease.
There are on this mountain other demons, more powerful still: / rākṣasas, piśācas, and exceedingly dreadful female piśācas.

Wandering from forest to forest, according to their past deeds, / they somehow and somewhere find food and drink.

Having heard this: "Let there be no fear for you from them here; / they are not able even to look upon you, pure and devoted to Govinda.
Him whose armor is devotion to Viṣṇu, who is wholly devoted to Nārāyaṇa, / rākṣasas, ghosts, and pūtanās do not touch, nor do they look upon."
bhūtas, vetālas, gandharvas, śākinīs, āryakas, grahas, / revatīs, vṛddharevatīs, mukhamanḍīs, and evil spirits;
yakṣas, cruel bālagrahas, malevolent vṛddhagrahas, / terrible mātṛgrahas, and other vināyaka spirits;
kṛtyās, serpents, kūṣmāṇḍas, and whatever other evil creatures there be— / they do not look upon a noble, pure Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa.
Spirits protect the pure; they do not torment the righteous; / and the deities of the planets and asterisms continually protect the pure.
The name of Govinda is on the tip of your tongue; the Veda resides in your heart; / you are pure and generous; you have nothing to fear from anywhere.
Thus, O brāhmaṇa, I remain, experiencing the fruit of my karma; / reflecting again and again, I think: ‘I do not grieve.’
I did not sorrow so much until, as I wandered / on the bank of the Jambālinī, I heard the words spoken by a crane."
The brāhmaṇa said: / "What sort of words spoken by a crane were heard by you? / I wish to hear that; tell me quickly, O preta!"
The preta said: / "I will tell the speech of the crane; listen, O best of pilgrims: / In this thicket named Dhūsarā, there is a river born of the mountain,
ever surging with bodies of water, crowded with rutting herds of elephants, / rich in the beauty of great kakubha trees, and charming with glossy jambū trees.
Penetrating the dense forest, I reached its bank. / While I was staying there with the desire of eating fruit,
a male crane, accompanied by his female mate, flew up from another part of the forest / and came with many birds to frequent the sandbank of the river.
Having drunk water right there and enjoyed himself with his wife, / he fell asleep, tucking his head and beak into his left wing-socket.
Meanwhile, descending from a tree, there was seen / a monkey with a red face and very red eyes, holding a staff, with a row of sharp claws,
hairy, with a long tail, and of restless movement; / he swiftly came to the spot where that crane was asleep.
Approaching, he seized the crane firmly by the leg / with his two hands, with cruel intent, while many birds looked on.
Flying up and away, all those birds went elsewhere; / but the female crane, terrified, stood making cries.
The crane, his sleep broken, his eyes rolling with terror, / quickly looked around, his neck trembling with agony.
Seeing the wicked monkey exceedingly eager to kill him, / the bird then addressed him in a sweet voice:
‘Why do you torment me when I am without fault, O monkey? / In the world, only those who have committed offences are slain even by kings.
Noble beings like you ought not to harm / us who are non-violent, virtuous, and averse to taking what belongs to others,
who eat water-moss, who fly in the air and live in the forest, / who delight in our own mates and shun the mates of others.
Those like you, O best of monkeys, ought not to torment / the twice-born who are devoted servants, free from reviling and slandering others.
O monkey, release me quickly; I am entirely blameless! / I know your birth, but you do not know mine.’
Hearing her words, the crane was then released; / the restless monkey quickly spoke, standing at a distance:
The monkey said: / ‘Tell me, how do you know my past birth? / You are a bird devoid of knowledge, and I am an animal roaming the forest.’
The crane said: / ‘I know your birth; clearly, I remember my past lives. / You were indeed the king and ruler of the Vindhya mountain in a past life.
I was the most venerable brāhmaṇa, the priest in your lineage; / therefore, O best of monkeys, I recognise you well.
While ruling this earth, all the subjects were oppressed by you, / devoid of discernment, as you accumulated wealth excessively.
O monkey, by the flames of the fire arising from the torment and agony of the subjects, / you were burnt earlier, and then cast into the most dreadful Kumbhīpāka hell.
Repeatedly burnt and repeatedly reborn / with a hellish body, thirty years passed for you,
as you uttered terrible sounds and wept again and again; / indeed, sharp torments were endured by you in the fire of Kumbhīpāka.’
Having crossed over hell, now, due to the remainder of your sins, / you have obtained birth as a monkey, in which you wish to kill me.
In the past, from a brāhmaṇa's garden, ripe plantain fruits indeed / were eaten by you without permission, having seized them by force.
Behold the terrible ripening of that karma bearing fruit: / by that you now exist as a monkey living in the forest.
Of evil and also of good action done in the past, / the fruition plays out among beings; it cannot be transgressed even by the gods.
Thus I know your birth accurately, together with its cause; / though I have acquired a crane's body, I am not confounded by ignorance.
The ghost said: / Hearing this speech, O brāhmaṇa, the monkey also said to the crane: / “You surely know correctly. How did you come to be a bird?”
The crane said: / “I shall tell that deed by which I went to a wretched state, / by which I entered the womb of a bird. You should listen to all of that.
Formerly, a full hundred khārīs of grain was indeed given away by you / to many brāhmaṇas at Carmadā during a solar eclipse.
Deceiving the twice-born out of pride in my priesthood and out of greed, / having given them just a little, I took everything for myself.
From the sin born of taking property common to brāhmaṇas, / I fell into the Kālasūtra hell, which is filled with mud of blood,
completely full of crawling worms, foul-smelling, and frothing with pus. / Sunk there up to my navel, with face downwards, I licked pus.
Likewise eaten from above by great vultures and by crows, / and continually pricked by worms, my body [suffered].
In that mire of blood, I was then breathless; / even a single muhūrta became like a great kalpa to me there.
Torments were experienced by me for thirty thousand years; / and I am unable to describe that agony of hell, O monkey.
The priesthood is exceedingly terrible and by its very nature brings sin, / where the livelihood depends on the gods, and where it is the livelihood of a brāhmaṇa.
Accepting gifts from a king is terrible; by it the twice-born are burnt. / If the family priest takes even their wealth, he goes to hell.
Whatever sin a king commits is placed beforehand in his [priest's] body; / therefore he is declared by seers of truth to be the purohita of that [king].
Somehow, by chance, deliverance from the ocean of hell was obtained; / by the working of ill fortune, the state of a bird has come upon me.
In the past, having stolen a bronze vessel from my sister's house, / it was given by me to a gambler; because of that is my condition as a crane.
And this brāhmaṇa woman was formerly a terrible bronze-thief; / therefore she became a female crane, my lawful wife.
Thus, O monkey, the entire fruit of karma has been told to you, / both past and present; now hear the future.
I shall become a swan, and you also will become a swan; / and this wife of mine, now a female crane, will also become a female swan.
And in the region of Kāmarūpa we will dwell at our ease; / after that we will attain the auspicious future Yoginī [pīṭha].
And after that we will again obtain a human birth, which is hard to attain, / where ultimate good and its opposite are accomplished by living beings.
In this way Śiva, having deluded all creatures with his māyā, / causes them to experience pleasures and pains—not only us alone.
And this path set in motion in the world is manifoldly fashioned; / consisting exceedingly of dharma and adharma, its very essence is the fruits of happiness and sorrow.
It is frequented by all living beings, always, time and again— / by gods, asuras, humans, tigers, worms, insects, and water-dwellers.
Indeed, this path thorny with sorrow has been overcome by no one at all, / except detached yogins, meditating, who have crossed to the end of the Vedānta.
Whether of minute or great meritorious or unmeritorious deeds, / the Great Lord bestows here the fruit, taking into account the place and time.
Having thus known the māyā of the Lord, which knows the rules of destiny, / those of great intellect do not grieve, nor do they torment themselves, nor do they despair.
The fruition of past deeds cannot be altered / by stratagems, or by wisdom, O monkey, even by the gods.
Formerly you were born a king, and later you became an inhabitant of hell; / now you have become a monkey, and you will attain a birth conforming to that.
Thinking thus, free from grief, O monkey, wait at your ease / for the appointed time, delighting here in this forest.
I too, likewise bound by the māyā of the Lord, shall indeed pass away / my birth as a crane from forest to forest, taking recourse to fortitude.
The monkey said: / I worshipped you in the past, and I bow to you now as well; / you remember your past births, [and] I know all of my past embodiment.
Dwell [here], O excellent crane; may there always be auspiciousness for you. / Free from delusion by your word, I shall wander at all times.
The ghost said: / As this delightful, wondrous, and supremely purifying / conversation between bird and monkey was heard on the bank of the river, O twice-born,
just then understanding arose in me too, and grief was destroyed thereby. / Now, having seen the supremely wondrous glory of the water of the Jāhnavī,
here, O best of brāhmaṇas, I beg you for the water of the Jāhnavī. / Desiring to cross beyond the state of a ghost, I am sorely afflicted by thirst.
And indeed, an astonishing thing was seen by me on this very mountain, O twice-born, / of the water of the Gaṅgā; truly, I wish to drink that water.
A certain brāhmaṇa born in Pāriyātra, a village priest, / became a brahmarākṣasa in the Vindhya [mountains] because of performing sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice.
Coveting our company, he remained for eight years. / His bones were collected by his good son, O best of the twice-born,
and brought and thrown into the Gaṅgā at the immaculate sacred place Kanakhala; / that very moment he was freed from the terrible state of a rākṣasa.
Thus the wondrous greatness of bathing in the water of the Gaṅgā / was seen directly by me; therefore the water of the Gaṅgā was requested.
Because abundant gifts were accepted by me in sacred places in the past, / and no counteraction such as recitation [of mantras] was performed for it,
therefore, for me in the form of a ghost, food and water are hard to obtain, / where a thousand years have passed on the Vindhya mountain.
Thus everything has been told to you, casting off all great shame. / Now, O best among the righteous, quickly, by giving water,
gratify my vital breaths that cling merely to my throat! / Even in the state of a ghost, life is hard to obtain for living beings here.
For the body is to be protected by men by every means and at all times; / indeed, even those suffering from leprosy and other diseases do not desire to abandon the body.
Devadyuti said: / Having heard his speech, the traveler experienced great wonder, / and reflected, harboring compassion for the ghost:
'The fruit of sin and merit is indeed visibly seen in the world: / the state of gods, dānavas, humans, animals, worms, and insects;
births in various wombs, affliction by various diseases, / the death of the young and the old, blindness and crookedness,
sovereignty and poverty, scholarship and foolishness— / how else could these arrangements come to be in the world?
Fortunate are those in this realm of action who give wealth earned by righteous means / to worthy recipients and accomplish their own welfare!
Land, jewels, gold, cows, grain, houses, elephants, / chariots, horses, garments, villages, cooked food, fruit, water,
a maiden, divine medicine, food, an umbrella, shoes, an excellent seat, / a bed, betel, garlands, a palm-leaf fan, an excellent seat—
all this should be given by those who desire to conquer the three worlds. / For what has been given is obtained in heaven, and indeed what has been given is enjoyed.
Umbrellas, fly-whisks, vehicles, excellent horses, excellent elephants, / palaces, excellent beds, cows, buffaloes, excellent women,
food, ornaments, pearls, sons, maidservants, noble lineage, / long life, health, sovereignty, proficiency in arts and sciences—
all this is obtained by human beings on earth as the fruit of gift alone; / therefore one should give with effort; what has not been given is not available.'
This verse was sung by the righteous traveler. / Hearing this, the ghost, his mind distressed, spoke again:
'I think you are almost equal to a knower of dharma, O traveler; there is no doubt about this. / Give me water, the giver of life, as a cloud [gives rain] to the cātaka bird.
In this giving of life, do not delay long!' / Then the traveler replied with words pregnant with reason:
'Listen, O ghost: my two parents are staying in the Bhṛgu territory. / For their sake the water of the king of holy places was fetched by me.
That black-and-white water is requested on the way by you; / I do not know; there is a doubt about dharma; what is proper for me here?
In order to deliberate on the stronger and the weaker, I shall adopt a powerful rule / based on the Vedas and dharmaśāstras, not by mere opinion of mine.
The protection of the lives of living beings is considered by sages and deities / to be superior even to all sacrifices, such as the horse sacrifice.
having given this excellent water and protected the ghost, / taking pure water once more for my father's sake, I shall carry it away.
This seems to me a pre-eminent ordinance, bestowing pure dharma; / other than helping others, everything is considered trivial by the wise.
Even their lives have been given gladly by men who do good to others; / if doing good to another can be done by water, what then have I not gained?
This verse sung formerly by Dadhīci is heard on earth, / which is the essence consisting of all dharmas, approved by all knowers of dharma:
Benevolence to others should be performed even with one's life, even with one's wealth; / the merit born of benevolence to others is equal even to hundreds of sacrifices.”
Having spoken thus, that most righteous, excellent twice-born gave the water / born from the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā to the ghost to protect his life.
The pleased ghost, having drunk the water and sprinkled his head with it, / abandoned that ghost body and in an instant became one possessing a divine body.
Having seen that great wonder, that man from Kerala said: / 'Ah, he has been freed from the state of a ghost by drops of the water of the Confluence!
I consider that even Brahmā is not able to declare the virtue of these waters; / otherwise, how would Mahādeva bear the water of the Gaṅgā on his head?
He who drinks even as much as a sesame seed of the water of the Gaṅgā, possessing inconceivable power, / would become a god or a perfected being, and would not enter a womb at all.
There is no accomplishment equal to the Gaṅgā; there is no wisdom equal to the Gaṅgā; / there is no liberation equal to the Gaṅgā, because the Gaṅgā is superior to all.
Therefore, O righteous one, by every effort and with great devotion, / liberation is in the hand of him who constantly serves the Gaṅgā.
May you live long, O traveler! Do not turn away from dharma! / I have been delivered instantly by you through the gift of a drop of the water of the Gaṅgā.'
Having spoken thus, that piśāca from Kerala departed for heaven, / having greeted the traveler, that excellent man and kin, with blessings.

Having liberated the spirit, the traveler too took that water again
and went along that very path, recollecting the wonder of the holy water.

Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus hearing the glorification of Prayāga and bowing to that sage,
the piśāca quickly went to Prayāga in the month of Māgha.

Bathing in the dark and white [waters] in the month of Māgha, O best of the twice-born,
the piśāca, his sins diminished, cast off his piśāca body.

Becoming a divine-bodied Dravidian king at that time,
he praised the god Nārāyaṇa with devotion, freed from faults.

Praised by gandharvas and honored by heavenly women,
he went to Indra's city on an excellent celestial chariot.
Thus have I told you, O vipra, the curious past event, / a legendary history, O best of the twice-born, that immediately destroys sins.

It grants knowledge and liberation, O brāhmaṇa, and when heard it destroys misfortune.
Thus I have told you all the wondrous past event,
The legendary history that destroys misfortune has been heard, O best of the twice-born; / now, together with me, these maidens and your son—

and you yourself, must go to Prayāga, all desirous of a good state.
Let us perform the bath of Māgha here, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
There they will immediately be freed from the piśāca-state born of sin.

Maheśa said:
Thus joyfully drinking the sweet nectar of the story from the lotus mouth of Vasiṣṭha,
all were delighted, having crossed the ocean of hell.

Together with him they quickly departed in the sky, gladdened.
O Dilīpa, hear all about that holy place of the dark and white [waters].

Quickly along the path of the sky, having attained their desire, those hard to endure
arrived there at that time, their hearts filled with delight.

Then Lomaśa spoke compassionately there in the courtyard of the sky:
"Let all behold with faith this king of holy places on earth.

Even without knowledge, all creatures are liberated here at Prayāga.
Having sacrificed with a great sacrifice right here, the Lord of Creatures, wishing to create,

obtained the power of creation, and then he performed creation.
Here Nārāyaṇa bathed in the dark and white [waters], desiring a wife.

Hence he obtained Lakṣmī as his wife during the churning for nectar.
And having dwelt here for six months and bathed in the Veṇī at will,

the trident-bearer [Śiva] destroyed Tripura with three arrows.
These are three pools illuminated by ceaseless fires.

This fire has attained satisfaction, which flourishes by whatever means.
Here the thirty-three gods, satisfied, rejoiced greatly.

Here Maheśa appeared, blue-throated, carrying a skull.
Constantly to be served by the gods, a youth arrived for the sake of the water offering.

He in whose mouth the son of Mṛkaṇḍu [Mārkaṇḍeya] entered and stayed during the cosmic cycle,
when the world was overwhelmed with flames, is this Janārdana, having the form of yoga.

This is the Bhāgīrathī of Śambhu, which removes all sorrow;
she is resorted to by the perfected for the sake of accomplishment, granting the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.

She ceaselessly bestows prosperity and is unsurpassed on the path to heaven;
she is the cause of heaven, this river Bhāgīrathī.

By merely bathing in whose waters all creatures obtain
the realm of the sun [Vikartana], that river is Yamunā herself.

The confluence of these two holy rivers brings happiness, O sage.
Those who have bathed here are not cooked in hell, their minds imbued with knowledge.

Even without knowledge, all creatures are liberated at this Prayāga.
Furthermore, let another ancient legendary history be heard, O brāhmaṇa,

which destroys all sins and all diseases for those who hear it.
Formerly, cursed by Ṛcīka, a gandharva became a crow.

He was released from the curse right here as soon as he bathed in the dark and white [waters].
By the curse of Vāsava [Indra], the apsaras Urvaśī fell from heaven;

desiring heaven, she bathed and thereupon attained heaven after a long time.
And Yayāti the son of Nahuṣa obtained Śaṃkara as a son, O sage,

desiring a son, after bathing at Prayāga in the auspicious dark and white [waters].
Formerly Śakra [Indra], desiring wealth, bathed well here, O best of the twice-born,

and by illusory power he carried off all the treasures of Dhanada [Kubera].
Here Kaśyapa performed austerities, intent on worshiping Śiva.

At this holy place Bharadvāja attained success in yoga.
At this holy place formerly, O brāhmaṇa, the masters of yoga whose minds were serene,

Sanaka and the others, attained the fertile ground of yoga's fruit.
Those who have bathed in this month of Māgha at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā

have assumed the forms of stars, and by them the entire universe is pervaded.
Those who have desires obtain their desires; seekers of liberation attain liberation.

Practitioners attain accomplishment at Prayāga, O best of the twice-born.
Now let these maidens who desire liberation, and also your son,

and you yourself, bathe here at my word in the dark and white [waters].
By the power of the water of the Veṇī, which destroys past sins,

let them obtain all glory whose great fruit was acquired through their curse."
Having thus heard the truthful words of the sage, beyond the senses and not to be transgressed,

they, with hearts filled with longing, all prepared to bathe.
Reaching Prayāga, which is hard to reach, they cast off their piśāca-state in an instant.

Released from the sorrow of the curse, they each regained their own form.
Seeing his son and those maidens of divine form,

Vedanidhi praised Lomaśa with affection and a serene inner self:
"By your grace alone the great ocean of sin has been crossed.

Now tell what is proper for these youths, O best of the sages."
Lomaśa said:
"This youth has studied the Vedas and completed his observances; he is a young man.

Let him take the lotus hand of these [maidens] who are full of love."
Then, by the word of Lomaśa and by the word of his own father,

that righteous student of the Veda quickly, according to the rule of marriage,
with auspicious items, mantras, and blessings performed by the sages,

took the hands of all five maidens according to dharma.
Then all the maidens became joyful, their desires fulfilled,

and that youth also became satisfied.
Having given his permission, that sage Lomaśa, bowed to by them,

went to his own hermitage on Mount Meru, frequented by the gods.
Then, O king, Vedanidhi, having placed his five daughters-in-law and his son in front,
went joyfully to the city of Dhanada [Kubera].

Thus, O best of kings, from the merit produced by bathing in Māgha, by the words of the best of sages, at Prayāga, the king of sacred fords, / freed instantly from all impurities, the five Gandharva maidens attained their desires from the abundance of their gained reward, and departed.

Whoever constantly hears this supreme, purifying, holy legendary history,
which is the cause of the destruction of sin, in this world,
becomes truly filled with all desired longings, and endowed with dharma goes to the world of the gods, which is hard to attain.
Whoever, having heard this legendary history, honors the reciter / with cows, gold, and garments, is indeed equal to Brahmā.

when the speaker is honored, Viṣṇu is honored.
Therefore, one should worship him daily if one desires fruitful existence.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, entitled "The Marriage of the Gandharva Maidens," in the glorification of Māgha, in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.

6.129.m: Pārvatī said: / “The glorification of Kārtika and that of Māgha have been heard by me, O Lord. / Now I wish to hear of the supreme action that bestows liberation.
What devotion is declared to be the best? Tell me, O Lord, Sovereign of the universe, / by the mere knowledge of which men may attain happiness.”
Mahādeva said: / “When that man's mind is absorbed in Him, that devotion is considered supreme: / always devoted to the virtue of compassion, intent on the duties concerning Viṣṇu,
eating fruits, roots, and water, bearing the conch and disc, / one should worship Viṣṇu at the three junctures of the day; that devotion is deemed sāttvika.
The sāttvika is declared highest, the rājasa is middle, / and the tāmasa is the lowest: thus threefold devotion is described.
It should be performed toward Śrīdhara by those desiring liberation as a fruit. / With egotism, beauty, ostentation, malice, and deception,
the devotion which people perform is cited as tāmasa; / or for the destruction of another, or aiming at ostentation,
whatever devotion is performed toward God is proclaimed to be tāmasa. / Aiming at sensory objects, or fame, or even sovereignty,
whoever worships me in an image and the like with a sense of separateness is rājasa. / For the exhaustion of karma, it should be performed by brāhmaṇas intent on knowledge.
The disposition of self-surrender unto Viṣṇu—that devotion is considered sāttvika. / Therefore indeed, O goddess, Hari must be served in every way and at all times.
By a tāmasa disposition, a tāmasa state is indeed obtained; / a rājasa [disposition] leads only to the rājasa, but by a sāttvika one, a sāttvika [state is gained].
Delighting in the study of the Veda, glorious, free from passion and hatred, / bearing the conch and disc, a brāhmaṇa is declared to be ever pure.
He who is engaged in the ritual section and is always a reviler of Viṣṇu, / and a reviler of His people, is called a great outcaste.

Those who are ever devoted to Vedic study, ever sacrificers in sacrifices, / ever intent on the agnihotra, but averse to the duties concerning Viṣṇu / and revile the duties concerning Viṣṇu, are outside the Veda, O queen of gods.
The gods, overjoyed, bestow peace; grandfather Pitāmaha and others bestow safety; / the foremost chiefs of sages grant well-being to men who bear devotion to Govinda.
Auspicious are the planets along with spirits and piśācas; Brahmā and the hosts of gods are pleased; / and Lakṣmī remains steadfast in the home of men who bear devotion to Govinda.
Gaṅgā, Gayā, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, / Kāśī, Prayāga, and Kurujāṅgala / dwell in the body accompanied by devotion previously performed, for men who bear devotion to Govinda.
Thus the wise man should worship the Blessed Lord along with Śrī; / he will always have accomplished his purpose, that brāhmaṇa, there is no doubt here.
Whether a kṣatriya, or a vaiśya, or a śūdra, O best of gods, / by performing devotion especially, that person indeed attains liberation.”

6.130.m: Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, entitled "Description of the Greatness of Devotion to Viṣṇu," in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.

having enjoyed all pleasures there, they go to the eternal [abode] of Viṣṇu. / This great form ever removes sin.

Ah, the glorification of Viṣṇu is wondrous and hair-raising! / Even spontaneous remembrance is a granter of liberation in three ways.

Not by abundant wealth, nor likewise by vast learning, / but by the single yoga of devotion alone is he seen near in an instant.

Though standing near, he is far, like collyrium upon the eyes; / by the yoga of devotion, the Eternal One is visible to his devotees.

One thinks: 'This is the reality, this is the reality,' deluded by divine māyā; / when the reality of devotion is obtained, then the world consists of Viṣṇu.

Nectar was obtained by Indra and the others for the sake of happiness, listen, O beautiful one; / even so they are distressed indeed, just as without devotion to Viṣṇu.

6.130.m:
Having obtained devotion alone as nectar, sorrow does not arise again; / having attained the abode named Vaikuṇṭha, one rejoices in the presence of Viṣṇu.

Just as the swan leaves the water and constantly drinks milk, / so, abandoning other duties, one should take refuge in devotion to Viṣṇu.

Abandoning devotion to others, one should take refuge in devotion to Viṣṇu; / having tied up water with a cloth, how could an end be accomplished?

Having obtained a body, [action] without devotion is done as wasted toil. / Those people who teach duties without devotion to Viṣṇu / fall perpetually into a dreadful hell; there is no doubt in this.
Just as a fool wishes to cross the ocean with his two arms, / so does a man [wish to cross] the ocean of worldly existence without devotion to Viṣṇu.
And if they protect devotion to Viṣṇu, [yet] one is brought low by action, / [he is like] a destitute man full of longing who directs his desire toward Mount Meru.
Even so, O goddess, a longing is made by me for your devotion; / for in another birth that devotion of mine brings about [liberation].
Just as here a fire, though very small, burns up a vast forest, / even so is that devotion, [even if] performed by me merely to the size of an atom.
Devotion is heard by hundreds, and understood even by thousands; / yet among them, O queen of gods, only a single devotee is born.
Many kinds of people in the world will give advice to others; / but the man who personally practices it is seen [only] among millions.
Devotion is attained through worship; it is brought about through victory. / When such a disposition exists, O queen of gods, devotion is grasped by that alone.
Just as a descent into the ocean [or] sitting down for safety in a well [is accomplished], / so he whose inner disposition is [firm] grasps that devotion.
When a tree is watered at the root, the foliage is seen upon the branches; / from adoration alone, O goddess, the fruit is established in front.
Just as a water-bearer fixes her mind upon the water-pot, / so, having fixed the mind upon the god Hari, one would attain liberation.
And just as in childhood a mother gives a little molasses, / and the boy begs again for molasses because of longing;
as water cast into water, milk into milk, or clarified butter into clarified butter [is merged], / even so, by the grace of devotion to Viṣṇu, they see no difference.
Just as the sun is omnipresent, and as fire is omnipresent, / so the devotee established in devotion is not bound at all by rituals.
Ajāmila, having abandoned his own duty and practicing sin, / remembered his son Nārāyaṇa and truly attained liberation with certainty.
And those devotees who day and night live by the name alone / are truly dwellers in Vaikuṇṭha; the Vedas are indeed witnesses to that.
The fruit of sacrifices like the horse sacrifice is seen even in heaven; / but having completely experienced that fruit, they surely fall down.
So, O goddess, having experienced pleasures in many ways through devotion to Viṣṇu / or having attained Vaikuṇṭha, when is there any return for them?
He by whom devotion to Viṣṇu is performed dwells in the world of Viṣṇu; / behold the example, O queen of gods, through the grace of devotion to Viṣṇu:
Hundreds of stones standing in the water were brought across by him; / [like] a moonstone without water is the mind of a devotee of Viṣṇu.
The frog dwells in the water, but the bee in the distant forest / perceives the fragrance of the night-lotus; even so is the devotee in devotion to Hari.
Some dwell on the bank of the Gaṅgā, while others are a hundred leagues away; / someone knows the fruit of the Gaṅgā, and another [knows] devotion to Viṣṇu in the same way.
A camel constantly carries a load of camphor and aloe wood, / [yet] does not know the fragrance within; so are those turned away from Viṣṇu.
Deer sniff the śāla tree, desiring the scent of musk, / [yet] do not know it resides in their own navel; so are those turned away from Viṣṇu.
Instruction given to fools is utterly in vain, O daughter of the mountain; / just so is instruction in devotion to Viṣṇu given to one turned outward.
When milk is drunk by a snake, that milk turns into poison; / just so does devotion to Viṣṇu turn into poison for devotees of others.
Just as those without eyes, having looked toward a lamp and a mirror, / do not see what stands near them, so those turned outward do not see Viṣṇu.
Just as fire is covered by smoke, and a mirror by dust, / and as an embryo is enveloped by the amnion, so Kṛṣṇa is veiled in the body.
Just as clarified butter is present in milk, and oil is always in sesame seeds, / so Viṣṇu is in the moving and unmoving, [yet] is not seen, O daughter of the mountain.
Just as many gems are held upon a single thread, / so this universe, beginning with Brahmā, is strung upon the spiritual Brahman.
Just as fire dwelling in wood is seen only through churning, / so Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, is seen only through meditation.
There may be a single original lamp, and from it thousands are produced; / in the same way, Viṣṇu stands alone, pervading all.
Just as at sunrise the light is always present in the sky, / and is seen manifoldly in water, so is Viṣṇu in the world.
Though staying in nature, the wind continually carries various fragrances; / the Lord, dwelling in all living beings, experiences the qualities born of nature.
Just as water becomes whatever it is through combination with sugar or poison, / so the self, having become involved, experiences the fruit of action.
And the earth, through union with water, produces various trees; / through contact with the qualities of nature, it is born in various wombs.
In an elephant or in a mosquito, in a god or in a human being, / it is neither greater nor lesser; it remains firm and motionless in the body.
From Brahmā down to a clump of grass, whatever humans are here on earth, / the gods, sacrifices, and serpents, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and others—
in all of them [reflections] are seen like that of the moon in water; / he is seen as Śiva, being, consciousness, and bliss, the Great Lord.
He indeed is declared to be Viṣṇu; he is that omnipresent Hari, / known through the Vedānta, the Lord of all, beyond time, free from affliction.
Whoever knows Revanta, O goddess, he is a devotee—of this there is no doubt. / For the One is to be known as manifold, and the manifold is indeed only One.
He is spoken of in various ways on earth by distinctions of name and form; / the eye sees through the light of the sun, and by the sun the eye flourishes.
So are the Supreme Self and the individual self always in every body; / just as space is in pot after pot, remaining as it was when that is broken,
so are you in form after form, utterly motionless when that is broken; / just as a wooden form collapses without a master,
the body made of various worms collapses without the self; / the colors of gold [change], but through fire they return to their former state;
similarly, individual souls attain their original form through devotion; / covered by their own cloud, fools see the sun as devoid of light;
so those whose minds are clouded by ignorance do not know that Lord; / he is recited by the Vedāntas as without conceptual construct, formless.
And from the formless he appears as possessing form by his own will; / from him space was born, soundless and devoid of qualities.
From space the wind was born, and it then became possessed of sound; / from the wind light was born, and from light water came to be.
In that water was the golden womb, the cosmic person bearing the universal form, / and in his navel-lotus are tens of millions of cosmic eggs.
From him came primordial nature and the person; the threefold world was made; / from the union of those two, the combination of principles was born.
Viṣṇu's manifestation is pure goodness; Brahmā is traditionally known as passion; / Śiva is declared to be darkness; by these everything is set in motion.
There is a single state of Brahmā in the world, according to the seed of actions; / by that, Viṣṇu dissolves all worlds without remainder.
The imperishable Lord Viṣṇu remains there at that time; / thus Viṣṇu is omnipresent, the beginning, the middle, and the end.
Through ignorance people do not know, being fixed on ritual action; / whoever performs actions appropriate to their caste at proper times,
that action whose deity is Viṣṇu is certainly not a cause of entering the womb; / in the Vedānta scripture, this is always deliberated by the sages.
This is knowledge of Brahman in the body; that I now proclaim. / The mind alone is the effect and the cause of both good and evil.
When all is purified by the mind, then eternal Brahman [is attained]. / The mind alone is always a friend, the mind alone is always an enemy.
Some are saved by the mind, and some are tormented by the mind. / Renunciation of everything within, while performing action outwardly,
one acting thus is not tainted even while performing action, / just as a lotus leaf is not tainted even by drops of water.
As fire thrown into fire, so what need is there with devotion? / When the nectar of devotion is known, liberation is not relished then.
Viṣṇu cannot be attained by the eightfold yoga in this birth; / or rather, Viṣṇu is attained through devotion, [by which] he is always easily attained.
Knowledge is attained through the Vedāntas, and through knowledge the object to be known is attained. / When that object to be known is attained, then this world is empty.
Viṣṇu is not attained by force, and what use are the eightfold yogas? / Purity of inner disposition is praised above all states.
Just as a beloved woman is embraced, so the fruit corresponds to one's disposition. / Indeed, a foot shod with a shoe perceives the earth as made of leather.
In whatever manner one's intellect is, in that manner one considers the world. / Even if watered with milk, a neem tree does not abandon its bitter nature.
Creatures follow their innate nature; instruction is useless. / Having cut down a mango tree, how can one obtain fruit or leaf?
Why should one waste a birth for the sake of the pleasure of the senses? / Just as medicine is cooked in a pot made of lapis lazuli,
and the remedy is burnt up, so why should a birth be in vain? / And having placed a treasure in the house, how could a fortunate person perform servitude?
Having abandoned the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, how could one delight in another path? / What is the use of the four Vedas studied devoid of devotion?
Even a dog-cooker endowed with devotion is worshipped even by the thirty [gods]. / Having bound a bracelet on one's own wrist, what is the use of mirrors?
And the servants whose sovereignty was granted by gods such as Brahmā and Rudra, / do not take anything offered by the Lord.
He did not go to give a boon to a devotee who possessed nothing. / How could there be meditation on bodyless Kṛṣṇa?
Many, having beheld the embodied form, have gone to that realm through devotion. / How can worship and devotion be directed toward the void? The wise speak of the embodied form.
How does a man walk upon the empty path without a support? / He who has form is himself the master; the formless is indeed the Lord.
He who has form is easily seen; the formless is not seen. / The sweetness of service is with the embodied; with the formless there is no flavor.
By means of the embodied, the formless is known spontaneously. / When one's body thrills with hair standing on end by grace of the remembrance of Hari,
and joyful tears fill the eyes, then liberation becomes a handmaid. / How does the sin committed in childhood not perish
through worship, gifts, vows, sacred fords, recitations, and burnt offerings dedicated to you? / Abandoning one's own dharma, how could one perform severe austerity?
Death in one's own dharma is better; another's dharma brings fear. / Forsaking the scriptural ordinance, how could one perform severe austerity?
Without an stage of life, the foolish man cannot attain perfection. / The castes were created by Brahmā, appointed each to its own dharma.
Wealth acquired through one's own dharma is called white wealth. / A gift given with faith using white wealth,
even if small, yields great religious merit; there is no count to it. / Wealth brought for household deeds through association with the base,
the gift given with that wealth by human beings and others / does not bear fruit for them; they do not partake of that fruit at all.
Whatever sort of action a person performs desiring the pleasure of the senses, / into that sort of womb the foolish man, weak in knowledge, enters.
Whatever action one performs here is experienced in the other world. / If suffering arises for a man who practices virtue,
then sorrow should not be felt; that is an action born of a former body. / And when suffering arises for a man who practices sin,
joy should not be felt in that pleasure, O ruler of the gods! / And just as beasts bound with ropes by a master at his will,
so men on the earth are led by the bondage of action. / A monkey living in the forest dances from house to house,
and in this way living beings are led by action into all wombs. / Just as a ball is driven at will by a playing master,
so a creature is led by action into pleasure and pain. / A living being bound by its own actions is unable to restrain the bondage.
Even gods are bound by actions, and likewise other sages. / The poison-eating serpents on Rudra's body on Kailāsa
are unable to drink nectar; the womb of action is very powerful. / He who grants a healthy body is indeed called the Sun by the wise,
yet the charioteer of his chariot is lame; the womb of action is very powerful. / Indradyumna, the royal sage, attained elephant-hood through action.
By the capable master, the womb of action in him was made void. / The gods headed by Rudra and Brahmā, and the humans and asuras who exist,
all of them, bound by action, wander upon the surface of the earth. / The entire world, subject to action, was created long ago by Viṣṇu.
That action is subject to Keśava; it is destroyed by the name of Rāma. / Water is found everywhere, yet it gives liberation at the confluence of the white and black [rivers].
Thus for those who act, the worship of Keśava grants liberation. / He who performs action with the mind for the sake of the pleasure of the senses,
might consider the body alone through egotism. / A creature, remembering with the mind, should perform atonement;
he is the experiencer of past action, and action does not increase in the future. / Some praise the planets, some ghosts and goblins,
some praise the gods, and some speak of herbs; / some speak of mantras and perfection, and some of intelligence and valor;
some speak of effort, daring, fortitude, and likewise policy and strength. / All follow desires through praises of ego-driven action.
This is my settled conviction, as taught by the ancient wise: / when a creature is full of merit and no sin exists [in him],
Knowledge is twofold, and then merit becomes auspicious. / One whose sin and merit are equal, for him action exists.
when yoga and the pairs of opposites are equal, then he attains the state of bliss. / Renouncing all externally, he should be full of longing in his mind.
his conduct is useless, and because of that, such people experience sin. / If one performs actions externally, yet is desireless in mind,
that renunciation should be known as intermediate; he does not attain the full fruit. / Having renounced both externally and internally, relying upon the void through intellect,
that renunciation should be known as the highest, rare even for yogins. / Some abandon everything out of anger; some, under the influence of dispute;
some abandon everything out of hardship; all such renunciations are merely intermediate. / Endowed with right intellect and faith, not fallen under the sway of anger and the like,
a person, even though untouched by actions, goes to a good state. / In the house of the pure and prosperous, of the wise and of yogins,
one fallen from yoga is born in a family preceded by the twice-born; / and in a very short time he attains complete yoga.
One may go to the realm of consciousness and bliss through the grace of yoga and devotion. / Just as mud [cannot be washed away] by mud, or blood indeed by blood,
how can one wash away action by violent action? / How can a sacrifice, which consists of violent action, destroy action?
Sacrifices performed out of desire for heaven bestow little happiness in heaven; / and pleasures, though many, are impermanent.
There is no eternal happiness in them anywhere without devotion to Hari. / The happiness of universal rule, kingship, and likewise happiness in heaven—
I desire nothing else; I fear dwelling in the womb. / A stone indeed is broken by iron, but a ruby is not broken;
devotion to Viṣṇu, full of various desires, is not broken by the intellect. / A crane eats creatures living in water, but avoids frogs and the like;
likewise Yama, the killer of all, avoids the servants of Kṛṣṇa. / He who protects and destroys is indeed called the protector.
Where they dwell in their own place, burdened with hundreds of offenses, / Kṛṣṇa is merciful to one who has committed offenses;
and if he attains the fruit, what can the protector do? / Thus the Self in this body, dependent on another, is merciful.
The other shore was reached slowly; accompanied by wrestlers, it was not reached. / The giver of liberation to the hunter, he himself ferried Kubjā across.
Hard to reach even in a dream by Brahmā and others, he was easy to reach in the cowherd's house. / When he ate the leftovers of the cowherds, then they were ferried across by him.
The supreme Self, Janārdana, is constantly sung by yogins. / Seeing the imperishable, glorious Puruṣa, they [stood] in wonder, O goddess.
Those who recite this divine remembrance day by day, / freed from all sins, go to the eternal [realm] of Viṣṇu.

चांद्रंचंद्रप्रदेशेतुरमणंतीर्थनायकम्

तीर्थंअभयदंनामामृताख्यंविंध्यकंधरे

वैगलेयंप्रचंडायांचांडिकंमरकंटके
सोमेश्वरंतथातीर्थेप्रभासेपुष्करंतथा
देवमात्रंसरस्वत्यांपारावततटेस्थितम्
महालयंमहापद्मेपयोष्ण्यांपिंगलेश्वरम्
सिंहिकायांतथातीर्थंसौरवेरविसंज्ञकम्
कार्तिकंकृत्तिकाक्षेत्रेशांकरंशंकरेगिरौ
उत्पलाख्यंततोदिव्यंसुभद्रासिंधुसंगमे

जालंधरेततःप्रोक्तंतीर्थंविष्णुमुखंचयत्

अच्छोदेविष्णुकामंतुधर्मकामार्थमोक्षदम्

6.130.d:
चिंतयामिमहादेविविद्वत्संस्थोजनार्दनम्
अष्टोत्तरंतुतीर्थानांशतमेतदुदाहृतम्
योजपेच्छृणुयाद्वापिसर्वपापैःप्रमुच्यते
एषुतीर्थेषुयःस्नात्वापश्येन्नारायणंहरिम्
सर्वपापविनिर्मुक्तोयातिविष्णोःसनातनम्
जगन्नाथंमहातीर्थंलोकानांपावनंस्मृतम्
येगच्छंतिनरश्रेष्ठास्तेपियांतिपरांगतिम्
शताष्टकंमहापुण्यंश्रावयेत्पितृकर्मणि
इहलोकेसुखंभुक्त्वायातिविष्णोःसनातनम्
गोदानेश्राद्धदानेवाअहन्यहनिवापुनः
देवार्चनविधौविद्वान्परंब्रह्माधिगच्छति
वेत्रवत्यास्तुमाहात्म्यंवक्ष्यामिशृणुसुंदरि
यत्रस्नात्वाविमुच्यंतेयावदाभूतसंप्लवम्
वृत्रेणचकृतःकूपोमहागंभीरसंज्ञकः
कूपात्सानिःसृतादेवीमहापापौघनाशिनी
यथागंगातथेयंचसरिच्छ्रेष्ठासुरोत्तमे
अस्यादर्शनमात्रेणपापौघाःशमयंतिच
शृणुदेविप्रवक्ष्यामिइतिहासंपुरातनम्
यच्छ्रुत्वापापिनोदोषैर्विमुक्ताःकर्मबंधनात्
6.130.m:
Viṣṇu, Janārdana, the lord of all, residing among the wise. / This one hundred and eight sacred bathing-places have been declared.

Whoever recites or hears [this] is completely freed from all sins. / Having bathed in these sacred bathing-places, whoever sees Nārāyaṇa Hari,

freed from all sins, goes to the eternal [realm] of Viṣṇu. / The great sacred place Jagannātha is remembered as the purifier of the worlds.

Those best of men who go [there] also attain the supreme state.
One should cause the highly meritorious one hundred and eight [names] to be heard during rites for the ancestors.

Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes to the eternal [abode] of Viṣṇu.
During the gift of a cow, or in offering a śrāddha, or day after day,

in the rite of worshiping the deity, the wise person attains the supreme Brahman.

I shall proclaim the glorification of the Vetravatī; listen, O beautiful lady,
bathing in which they are liberated until the dissolution of beings.

A well named Mahāgambhīra was constructed by Vṛtra;
from that well emerged that goddess who destroys multitudes of great sins.

As is the Gaṅgā, so is this excellent river, O best among the gods;
by the mere sight of her, the floods of sins are subdued.

Listen, O goddess, I shall relate an ancient legendary history,
hearing which sinners are freed from faults and the bondage of karma.

6.130.d:
चंपकेनगरेचैवराजाराज्यंकरोतिसः
सदादुष्टोदुष्टरूपोजनानांसप्रपीडकः
अधर्मोधर्मरूपश्चविष्णुनिंदापरायणः
देवद्विजनिहंताचआश्रमाणांविदूषकः
वेदनिंदापरःश्रीमान्मूर्खोवानिर्घृणःशठः
असच्छास्त्रेषुनिरतःपरदाराभिमर्शकः
विदारुणेतिनामाचसंजातोमूर्खएवच
कदाचिद्दैवयोगेनआगतस्तांनदींप्रति
आखेटकसमायुक्तःस्वयंकुष्ठीसुरेश्वरि
महापापादयंजातोब्राह्मणानांचनिंदनात्
वृथावादीदुरात्माचशठोवैनिर्घृणःपशुः
वेदनिंदारतोनित्यंगोशास्त्राणांप्रदूषकः
एवंविधोवनेभ्राम्यंस्तृषार्तःससुहृद्वृतः
अश्वादुत्तीर्यराजाऽसौजलंपीत्वागृहंगतः
तेनैवोदकपानेनगतंकुष्ठंनसंशयः
बुद्धिस्तुनिर्मलाजातातस्यराज्ञोविशेषतः
विष्णौभक्तिःसमुत्पन्नातदातस्यसुरेश्वरि
ततःप्रभृतिकालेनस्नानंवैकृतवान्सदा
निर्मलोबहुरूपाढ्योजातस्तत्रसुरेश्वरि
इहलोकेसुखंभुक्त्वाकृत्वायज्ञाननेकशः
6.130.m:
In the city of Campaka, a king was ruling the kingdom;
he was ever wicked, wicked in appearance, and an oppressor of the people.

He was unrighteousness in the form of righteousness, intent on reviling Viṣṇu,
a killer of gods and twice-born, and a defiler of hermitages,

intent on reviling the Vedas, wealthy yet foolish, merciless, dishonest,
devoted to false scriptures, and an abuser of others' wives.

He was named Vidāruṇa, and he was indeed a fool.
Once, by the power of destiny, he came to that river.

Engaged in hunting, he himself had become a leper, O queen of gods;
this had arisen from a great sin—from reviling the brāhmaṇas.

He was an idle disputant, an evil-souled rogue, merciless, like a beast,
ever engaged in reviling the Vedas, and a defiler of cows and scriptures.

Wandering thus in the forest, afflicted with thirst and surrounded by his companions,
that king dismounted from his horse, drank the water, and went home.

By that very drinking of water, his leprosy vanished without doubt;
and the intellect of that king especially became spotless.

Devotion to Viṣṇu then arose in him, O queen of gods.
From that time on, he regularly performed his bath.

6.130.m:
He became spotless and endowed with great beauty there, O queen of gods;
having enjoyed happiness in this world and performed many sacrifices,

and having given priestly gifts to the brāhmaṇas, he went to the realm of Viṣṇu.
Knowing this, O goddess, especially regarding the Vetravatī,

those brāhmaṇas who bathe [there] are liberated, O daughter of the mountain;
whether a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra, O best among the gods,

wherever they bathe, they are liberated from the bondage of sin.
Whether in Kārttika or in Māgha, an outcaste or a reviler of the Vedas,

having bathed at the confluence of the rivers, O goddess, he is freed from sin.
Where her confluence with the Sābhramatī is seen,

having bathed especially there, a slayer of a brāhmaṇa is ever freed.
There is the heavenly city of Kheṭaka, having the nature of heaven, O sinless one.

Many yogas were performed there by Brahmā, O goddess;
having bathed and eaten there, there is no rebirth.

She is remembered as a second Gaṅgā, especially in the Kali age, O goddess.
Men who desire happiness, and men who desire wealth,

And those people who desire heaven, having bathed again and again, / and having enjoyed happiness in this world, go to the eternal [realm] of Viṣṇu.

and those born in the solar dynasty as well as in the lunar dynasty,
having come to the Vetravatī and bathed, attained supreme bliss.

6.130.m:
By the sight [of her], she takes away sorrow; by touch, she takes away mental sin;
having bathed and eaten, O goddess, one partakes of liberation, no doubt.

From bathing, recitation, and likewise from offering oblations, one attains endless fruit.
If, having gone to the sacred place of Vārāṇasī, one should practice the cāndrāyana vow with devotion,

great merit is attained by going there; but that same merit [is obtained], O best among the gods,
especially if one meets death in the Vetravatī.

Becoming four-armed, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Whatever sacred places there are on earth, whatever gods and ancestors,

all of them dwell here in the Vetravatī, O queen of gods.
What is the use of saying much more, again and again, O fair-faced one?

There is no sacred place on earth equal to the Vetravatī, O eternal one.
I, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the gods, and the supreme sages,

all the deities reside in the Vetravatī, O great goddess.
Those who perform bathing there once, twice,

or especially three times a day, are indeed liberated; there is no doubt.

I shall tell you, O goddess, the glorification of the Sābharmatī exactly as it is. / Kaśyapa, the best of sages, indeed performed great austerity.

6.130.m:
For many years great austerity was practiced by him
on the delightful Mount Arbuda, crowded with various trees.

Having gone there, austerity was performed by the sage Kaśyapa,
where the charming Sarasvatī is pure and destroys sins.

One day, O goddess, he went to Naimiṣa;
then all those sages held many conversations.

Then that sage Kaśyapa was properly asked by those twice-born:
"Ah, Kaśyapa! For our pleasure, let the Gaṅgā be brought here, O lord!

Bearing your name, she will become the best of rivers."
Having heard their words and bowed to those twice-born,

he came to the forest of Arbuda, near the bank of the Sarasvatī.
There he then performed extremely difficult austerity.

Indeed, I was propitiated by him, by the twice-born Kaśyapa;
and then I appeared visibly to that best of the twice-born:

"Choose a boon; may it be well with you; whatever is in your mind."

Kaśyapa said:
"You are capable of granting a boon, O god of gods, O lord of the universe!
This Gaṅgā, pure and removing sin, who resides upon your head,

should especially be given to me, O Mahādeva; reverence to you!"
Then, O goddess, it was said by me: "Take it, O best of the twice-born!"

Releasing one matted lock of hair, the Gaṅgā was then given by me.
Receiving her, the best of the twice-born went with joy to his own dwelling.

6.130.m:
The residence of Kaśyapa was a sacred place named Keśarandhra;
he went there, O queen of gods, surrounded by sages.

The Kāśyapī, that best of rivers, was brought along by Kaśyapa,
by the mere sight of whom even a slayer of a brāhmaṇa is indeed liberated.

Pārvatī said:
Tell me what merit comes merely from bathing in that sacred place,
O lord of the universe! You are compassionate; show mercy to me.

What merit is there from the sight, what from bathing? Tell me, O king of gods!
What is her greatness, O holy one? You should tell me everything.

Mahādeva said:
Many sacred places and sanctuaries have been heard of by me,
as well as rivers that flow to the ocean by the grace of the lord, glorious Viṣṇu:

The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Revā, and the great river Tāpī,
the Godāvarī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Kauśikī, and also the Gallikā,

the Kāverī, Vedikā, Bhadrā, and the sin-removing Sarayū,
and various other rivers on earth that take away all sins;

Prayāga, the king of sacred places, and Kāśī, and Puṣkara,
as well as the sacred place named the forest of Naimiṣa, and Amarakaṇṭaka.

The excellent sacred place of Dvārakā, and the excellent Arbuda forest, / and various divine sacred places of such kinds,

were heard of there, O queen of gods, by the grace of Māyāviṣṇu. / Formerly, indeed, I was beseeched by Bhagīratha, O Pārvatī;

then this Gaṅgā was given [to him] desiring the world of Viṣṇu. / By me, she was given again to Kaśyapa at the word of the sages.

This indeed is the Kāśyapī Gaṅgā, forever removing diseases and defects. / She who is spoken of in the world in each age by distinct names—

and at Kedāra and Kurukṣetra, whatever fruit is obtained from bathing— / that very fruit surely belongs to men day after day from the Sābhramatī.

There is no doubt that it is so, as is the word of Vyāsa. / In the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, or daily, O queen of gods,

whatever fruit there is in properly giving śrāddha on the new-moon day, / a man attains that fruit from immersing in the Sābhramatī.

On the full-moon day of Kārttika under the conjunction with Kṛttikā, at Śrīsthala before Mādhava, / a mortal obtains that fruit from immersing in the Sābhramatī.

6.130.m:
She is the greatest, O goddess, the purifier in all worlds; / she is most blessed, O goddess, pure, and a destroyer of sin.

On the Sābhramatī, indeed, these dwell continually: / those who were connected in the east, and those again in the north,

and westerners and southerners—all go continually / under the pretext of pilgrimage to Kheṭaka, into the presence of Brahmā.

They always come, O goddess, especially on the Kārttika full moon, without a doubt. / There they perform the śrāddha, and also feed the brāhmaṇas.

They practice various dharmas and continually perform various sacrifices; / and people always make various gifts there.

In all four cosmic ages, no doubt should be entertained here. / Yavakrīta, and Raibhya, and Kākṣīvat, and Uśij,

the descendants of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras, and Kaṇva, Medhāvin, and Punarvasu, / and Bandin, endowed with good qualities, took shelter in the eastern direction.

Those highly fortunate ones in the north, headed by Madhumat, / and the highly fortunate Subandhu, and the powerful Dattātreya,

Śikhin, Dīrghatamas, and Gautama, and Kaśyapa, / Śvetaketu, Kahoḍa, Pulaha, and Devala,

6.130.m:
Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, and the powerful Jamadagni, / the son of Ṛcīka, Garga, and the sage Uddālaka,

Devaśarman, Dhaumya, Āstīka, Kaśyapa, / Lomaśa, Nābhiketu, and Lomaharṣaṇa,

the sage Ugraśravas, and Cyavana the descendant of Bhṛgu, / and those headed by the Vālakhilyas—all indeed go there.

Having bathed, abstaining from food, always devoted to Viṣṇu, / bearing the conch, discus, and mace, they continually dwell on the bank.

The sacred place of the ancestors named Gayā, auspicious and the best among all sacred places, / where the lord of the gods, the Grandfather [Brahmā] himself, resides—

this verse was sung by the ancestors who desired a share of the śrāddha: / 'Many sons are to be desired, in case even one goes to Gayā!'

en:

And that which, through my presence, grants the fruit of enjoyment and liberation— / by my command, the lord of gods named Bindumādhava

dwells constantly, O queen of gods, especially in Vārāṇasī; / therefore, this city of mine is always the most blessed and supreme.

6.130.m:
The holy place beloved by the ancestors, holy Vimaleśvara indeed, / and the ancestral sacred place Prayāga, united with all sacred places,

come into the water of the Sābhramatī by my command, O goddess. / And the blessed lord Vaṭeśvara along with Mādhava,

holy Daśāśvamedhaka, and likewise Gaṅgādvāra— / by my appointment, O queen of gods, they dwell indeed in the Sābhramatī.

The river, then the goddess Lalitā, the sacred place called Saptadhāraka, / likewise Mitrapada by name, and Kedāra the abode of Śaṅkara,

and Gaṅgāsāgara, they say, which is auspicious and consists of all sacred places; / the sacred place Brahmasaras likewise, and in the pool of the Śatadru river,

and the sacred place named Naimiṣa—always by my command, / they dwell in the water of the Sābhramatī, O goddess, without a doubt.

The holy Śvetāvalkalinī, and then Śvetā, Hiraṇmayī, / Hastimatī, and Vārtaghnī, a river flowing to the ocean—

these are beloved by the ancestors, granting the fruit of ten million śrāddhas. / There śrāddhas should be offered by sons for the welfare of the ancestors.

The cities named Pāṭala and Vāḍava are there, O beautiful one; / these rivers have especially reached into the Sābhramatī forever.

6.130.m:
Those men on earth who perform bathing and gifting there, / having enjoyed happiness in this world, go to the eternal [abode] of Viṣṇu.

Jambūdvīpa is highly sacred, where merit increases; / therein is the highly sacred [tract] called Ārya, fulfilling all desires.

The sacred place known as Nīlakaṇṭha, and Nandahrada, / likewise Rudrahrada, and the holy Rudramahālaya,

the most holy Mandākinī, and the great river Acchodā— / these flow into the Sābhramatī, having made themselves visible.

Likewise Dhūmrā, Mitrapada, Baijnāth, the excellent stone, / the Kṣiprā river, Mahākāla, and the mountain Kāliñjara,

Gaṅgodbheda, Harodbheda, and Narmadākāra— / the wise declare them equal [to all shrines] through the offering of rice-balls in the Gaṅgā.

These holy places of Brahmā on the northern bank of the Sābhramatī / were kept hidden, O queen of gods, by the gods headed by Brahmā.

Even from memory, they destroy sins of the people, O great goddess; / how much more so for those mortals who give śrāddha, O queen of gods?

[…] the ancestral sacred place, and Kāverī, Kapilodaka, / and the confluence of the Caṇḍavegā, and likewise Amarakantaka—

6.130.m:
Silver, darbha grass, cows, a daughter's son, kutapa blankets, and sesame seeds; / sin is called 'bad' (kutsita), and they cause torment to it.

Since there are these eight, they are renowned as 'kutapa's. / After the kutapa muhūrta, the four muhūrtas,

and this period of five muhūrtas is desired for the time of a śrāddha. / Kuśa grass and black sesame are remembered as having arisen from the body of Viṣṇu,

for the protection of the śrāddha—so the gods have said. / A handful of water with sesame should be offered by those staying at a tīrtha, standing in the water,

with darbha in their hands; in this one way the śrāddha is not violated. / Entering the tīrthas on the Sābharmatī under their specific names,

having caused [it] to be made, O goddess, it was given by me to Kaśyapa. / That Kaśyapa is my devotee, ever dear to me.

Therefore, this pure Gaṅgā, destroyer of sins, was given [to him]. / On the Sābharmatī, O blessed lady, at the tīrtha called Brahmacārika,

having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes to the great abode of Śiva. / If one afflicted by severe diseases goes there,
